# Sirach Chapter 6 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Vaticanus, Sirach 6

---

1 Do not turn a friend into an enemy, for a bad name brings shame and reproach — such is the way of the double-tongued.

2 Do not exalt yourself by your own counsel, lest it tear you apart like a bull.

3 Your leaves will be devoured and your fruit destroyed, and you will be left like a dried-up tree.

4 An evil soul destroys the one who has it, and makes it a mockery to its enemies.

5 A pleasant manner multiplies friends, and a gracious tongue attracts many greetings.

6 Let those who wish you well be many, but let your counselors be one in a thousand.

7 If you want to make a friend, test him first; do not be quick to trust him.

8 For there is a friend who is such only for his own convenience, and will not stand by you in the day of trouble.

9 And there is a friend who turns into an enemy, who will expose your quarrel to your disgrace.

10 And there is a companion at the table who will not be found in the day of affliction.

11 When things go well for you, he will be like another self and make free with your servants.

12 But if you are brought low, he will turn against you and hide from your face.

13 Separate yourself from your enemies, and be on guard with your friends.

14 A faithful friend is a sturdy shelter; whoever finds one has found a treasure.

15 A faithful friend is beyond price; no scales can weigh his worth.

16 A faithful friend is a life-saving medicine; those who fear the Lord will find one.

17 Whoever fears the Lord makes true friendships, for as one is, so also is one's companion.

18 My child, from your youth receive instruction, and until your hair is white you will keep finding wisdom.

19 Come to her like one who plows and sows, and wait for her good harvest; for in cultivating her you will toil briefly, and soon you will eat of her produce.

20 How harsh she seems to the undisciplined! The senseless person cannot endure her.

21 She will weigh on him like a heavy stone of testing, and he will not be slow to cast her aside.

22 For wisdom lives up to her name; she is not accessible to many.

23 Listen, my child, and accept my judgment; do not reject my counsel.

24 Put your feet into her fetters and your neck into her collar.

25 Put your shoulder under her and carry her; do not chafe under her bonds.

26 Come to her with all your soul, and keep her ways with all your might.

27 Search her out, inquire and seek; she will make herself known to you. When you have hold of her, do not let go.

28 For in the end you will find the rest she gives, and she will be transformed into your joy.

29 Her fetters will become for you a strong defense, and her collar a glorious robe.

30 Her ornament is of gold, and her bonds are a cord of blue.

31 You will wear her like a robe of glory, and put her on like a crown of rejoicing.

32 If you are willing, my child, you can be taught; if you are diligent, you will become wise.

33 If you love to listen, you will gain knowledge; if you give your attention, you will become wise.

34 Stand in the assembly of the elders; and whoever among them is wise, attach yourself to him.

35 Be glad to hear every godly discourse, and do not let a saying of wisdom pass you by.

36 If you see a person of understanding, go to him early; let your foot wear out his doorstep.

37 Reflect on the statutes of the Lord, and meditate at all times on his commandments; it is he who will give insight to your mind, and your desire for wisdom will be granted.

---

## Council Notes

**On vv.14-16 — "faithful friend":** Ben Sira's threefold repetition of "faithful friend" (pistos philos) is one of the most celebrated passages in the book. SOPHIA preserves the anaphora. Each verse ends with a distinct characterization: shelter, beyond price, medicine.

**On vv.24-31 — the fetters paradox:** Ben Sira inverts the expected: what feels like chains (discipline, restraint) is revealed as glory (a robe, a crown). PNEUMA captured the emotional arc well. SOPHIA preserves EMET's structural fidelity.

**On v.19 — agricultural metaphor:** "One who plows and sows" — Ben Sira uses the farmer as the paradigm of patient, disciplined effort. The harvest is assured, but it takes time.

**On v.22 — "wisdom lives up to her name":** Greek paideia = "discipline/instruction," a word that also looks like "child" (pais). There may be a wordplay: discipline is like a child — she requires patience. EMET's "she is like her name" preserved.
